content_html:
The Peruvian Andes are full of fascinating stories that have been passed down from generation to generation. These legends not only reflect the worldview of ancient Andean civilizations, but also remain part of Peru's cultural identity. Here we tell you some of the best known:

1. The myth of the Ayar brothers and the founding of the Inca Empire

According to Inca mythology, four brothers and their wives emerged from a cave in Pacaritambo to found Tahuantinsuyo. Among them, Ayar Manco, with the help of the gods, managed to nail a golden rod into the fertile soil of the Cusco valley, marking the place where the great capital of the Inca Empire would be established.

2. The legend of the Apus, the gods of the mountains

The Apus are sacred spirits that protect the mountains and to whom we must pay respect. These stone giants are believed to guard Andean communities, protecting them from natural disasters and guiding travelers on their way. Many residents still leave them offerings in traditional rituals.

3. The myth of Lake Titicaca and the creation of the Andean world

It is said that Lake Titicaca is the origin of the Andean world. According to legend, the god Viracocha emerged from its waters to create the sun, the moon, the stars and the first humans. It is also believed that there are lost cities and hidden Inca treasures at the bottom of the lake.

4. The princess of snowy Salkantay and forbidden love

The story goes that the snow-capped Salkantay and the Verónica mountain were two young people in love, but their love was forbidden. As punishment, the gods turned them into separate mountains so that they could never be together. Today, the mountains remain distant, but it is said that on certain nights their souls try to find each other.

5. The legend of Supay, the god of the underworld

In Andean culture, Supay is the god of Ukhu Pacha (world below) and is associated with death and fear. Although in some regions he is seen as an evil spirit, in others he is considered a guardian of the balance between good and evil. In the Puno carnivals, it is represented with dances and colorful masks.
